title: Vector-lane branching and kernel divergence: quant bench notes (Nov 2026)
content:
Summary:

This note captures an experimental sweep focused on performance effects introduced by lane/warp divergence and branching inside quantized kernels. Motivation: several recent regressions in tail latency under mixed workloads appear correlated with kernels that implement per-block special-casing (e.g., residual scale handling, per-block zero-point masks, per-token gating). Hypothesis: variant code paths to handle outlier columns or activation masks produce branchy kernels that drastically reduce vector lane utilization on H100/A100, increasing tail latency even when average throughput is unchanged.

Goals:
- Measure the micro-impact on per-token latency and tail (95/99/99.9) when forward kernels include conditional paths for: per-block scaling, sparse-zero pruning, and mixed-quant fallback (FP32/FP16 for hot rows).
- Compare across quant schemes: INT8 symmetric/asymmetric, GPTQ (per-channel), AWQ (group-wise quant + per-group scale), and experimental FP8 block formats.
- Profile warps/lanes/TensorCore occupancy and quantify divergence penalties.
- Produce probative recommendations for kernel authors (e.g., favor masked vector ops vs conditional scalar repairs, preferred block sizes, and fallback thresholds).

Testbed and baseline:
- Hardware: NVIDIA H100 SXM (base) and A100 80GB for cross-checks.
- Runtime: local dev cluster build rti/serve:v1.44.0 (kernel ABI stable), CUDA 12.2, cuBLASLT experimental disabled to force our kernels.
- Models: distilled-7B and llama-13B distilled conv-opt checkpoints converted to our runtime formats. Models chosen to exercise different KV-cache densities and token sparsity.
- Workloads: synthetic steady-state generation (batch sizes 1, 4, 16), mixed QPS spike trace (90/10 short/long), and edge prompt set with many short prompts (1–8 tokens).
- Quality metric: small eval set perplexity + targeted MMLU slices for any catastrophic degradation checks. We log generation divergence rate (token-level mismatches against FP16 baseline) and regenerate costs.

Methodology and probes:
- We implemented microbench wrappers around forward kernels that emit hardware counters via nvprof/CUPTI and our in-process tracing (per-op start/end + kernel-block-level branch counts sampled via Nsight Perf).
- For each kernel variant we run a 30-minute steady-state trace capturing the following: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 latency, device-side branch-mispredict estimates, SM occupancy, tensor-core utilization, and achieved FLOPs.
- Kernel variants:
  * straight-line quant matmul (no repairs)
  * masked vector blend (branchless) where invalid columns are zeroed by an AND-mask
  * fallback scalar post-correction (branchy): compute vector chunk, then if outlier flag, run repair scalar path per lane
  * hybrid: group-wise quant but only repair top-k groups with branches
- We instrumented two block sizes: 32x128 and 64x64 (row-major tile) to see tiling effects on divergence.

Key numeric findings (representative):
- For distilled-7B, mixed-quant hybrid kernels (AWQ-groupwise with conditional fixes) exhibited average throughput decline of ~8% vs branchless AWQ, but p99 latency increased by 42% and p99.9 by 120% under the short-prompt workload (BS=1).
- Masked vector blend (branchless) had near-identical quality to branchy fallback (token mismatch delta < 0.25%), while maintaining p99 within 7% of FP16 baseline and p99.9 within 15%.
- GPTQ per-channel kernels implemented with per-channel branch checks (rare-scatter) produced the worst tail behavior: p99.9 increased 3-4x on H100 compared to branchless implementation. This was most visible when token sparsity increased (many zero-activation columns).
- For A100, divergence penalty was slightly lower (H100 shows larger discrepancy due to aggressive Tensor Core scheduling optimizations), but trends are consistent across both GPUs.

Profiling details:
- Occupancy: branchy kernels show nominal occupancy decreases of 10-18% in active warps due to serializing repairs on some threads in the block. Tensor core utilization drops correspondingly.
- Branch/mispredict: sampled branch mispredict counters increased by 5–12x for branchy repairs vs branchless blends.
- Memory stalls: conditional repairs tended to increase global memory stalls because repair path reads were not coalesced.

Quality tradeoffs:
- AWQ (groupwise) + branchless masked blend: quality delta vs FP16: +0.9–1.4% perplexity increase depending on group size (32–128). This is acceptable in many production configs.
- GPTQ (per-channel): better base quality (0.4–0.8%) but when we introduced aggressive group-fallback branches to correct high-residual columns quality advantage shrank and introduced tail-latency spike.
- FP8 experimental: single-pass FP8 kernels with no per-block repairs had slightly higher mismatch (1.8–2.5%) but superior tail latency (p99.9 comparable to FP16). FP8 shows promise where strict quality budgets allow.

Observations and actionable recommendations:
1) Favor branchless masking and vectorized repairs: when possible apply a precomputed mask + fused multiply-add with masked lanes zeroed. This preserves lane alignment and avoids warp divergence.
2) Reduce on-kernel scalar repairs: if repair must occur, move it to a separate post-processing step that runs asynchronously on a small thread pool (outside the hot kernel path) to avoid stalling warps.
3) Group-size tuning matters: larger group quant reduces repair incidence but increases per-group quant noise. Default 64-group AWQ gives good perf/quality sweet spot on H100 for our workloads.
4) Block tiling: 32x128 tiles presented fewer divergence hotspots for skewed activation distributions. Add this as a tunable in kernel registry.
5) Heuristic fallback thresholds: prefer probabilistic repair (sample top-k offending groups) instead of deterministic per-block branches; this preserves tail behavior with small quality hit.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Can we implement a hardware-friendly vector scatter for repairs that reduces non-coalesced loads? Probing vendor vector primitives in cuQL or upcoming CUDA releases may help.
- How do multi-tenant noisy co-run scenarios amplify divergence penalties? Need isolation experiments with mixed model sizes.
- Explore a lightweight in-kernel approximation for high-residual columns (e.g., low-rank correction) that is branchless.

Next steps / experiments planned:
- Patch branchless masked blend into the AWQ runtime path and run 72-hour production shadow at 10% traffic (dedicated lane) to collect true tail behavior under real prompts.
- Add telemetry to kernel registry so we can log per-request incidence of repairs (counts) and correlate with prompt characteristics.
- Prototype asynchronous repair worker and benchmark end-to-end latency/throughput in ramp tests.

Appendix: commands and probes used
- nv-nsight sampling: nsys profile --stats true -o out.nsys --sample=cpu,gpu --force-overwrite true --target-processes=all 
- simplified perf wrapper: python tools/kernel_probe.py --kernel awq_blend_mask --model distilled-7b --batch 1 --duration 1800 --trace-level hwcounters
- local occupancy quick-check: cuobjdump --dump-sass kernel.cubin | grep -A3 "OPCODE"  # used to eyeball warp-level flow

Notes to reviewers:
- I intentionally ran multiple seeds for prompt traces; raw traces and profiling folders are in GH artifact GH-rlwf/serve-kernels#412.
- This doc is a working note; suggestions for alternative kernel patterns welcome. If we agree on the branchless blending path, I'll open an RFC/PR for kernel change + rollout plan.

End.
